title: Nehemiah 3:1–14
context: Nehemiah 3 lists those who rebuilt Jerusalem’s wall and gates, beginning with Eliashib the high priest at the sheep gate and moving section by section around the city. Priests, Levites, district rulers, craftsmen, townspeople, and even a ruler’s daughters take part, while the Tekoite nobles refuse. Many gate and tower locations are uncertain, and reconstructions of the route and Jerusalem’s topography vary. Some names connect with the returnee lists of Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7. Both traditions read the list as shared ground about a whole community joining in God’s work.

verses.text: Then Eliashib the high priest rose up with his brothers the priests, and they built the sheep gate. They sanctified it, and set up its doors. They sanctified it even to the tower of Hammeah, to the tower of Hananel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eliashib the high priest and his fellow priests build and sanctify the sheep gate and set up its doors, as far as the towers of Hammeah and Hananel. The leaders begin.

Arminian readers see the priests modeling willing service.
verses.reformedNotes:
The sheep gate is usually placed north of the temple, though locations are debated. Eliashib the priest in 13:4 may or may not be the same man; the text does not say.

Reformed readers see work consecrated to God. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Next to him the men of Jericho built. Next to them Zaccur the son of Imri built.
verses.arminianNotes:
Beside them, the men of Jericho build, and next to them Zaccur son of Imri. Townspeople join priests.

Arminian readers see ordinary people freely taking up a share of the work, as Nehemiah had urged in 2:17–18.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God gathering his people from many places to one task. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the whole community’s part in restoring Jerusalem, with the men of Jericho taking their section of the wall.

verses.text: The sons of Hassenaah built the fish gate. They laid its beams, and set up its doors, its bolts, and its bars.
verses.arminianNotes:
The sons of Hassenaah build the fish gate, laying its beams and setting up its doors, bolts, and bars. The work is thorough.

Arminian readers see care taken over each part of the task.
verses.reformedNotes:
The fish gate’s name may reflect trade in fish brought into the city, though this is an inference, and its exact location is uncertain.

Reformed readers see faithful labor in ordinary details. Both traditions read this as shared ground about diligence in God’s work.

verses.text: Next to them, Meremoth the son of Uriah, the son of Hakkoz made repairs. Next to them, Meshullam the son of Berechiah, the son of Meshezabel made repairs. Next to them, Zadok the son of Baana made repairs.
verses.arminianNotes:
Meremoth son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz, Meshullam son of Berechiah, and Zadok son of Baana make repairs. Names follow one another.

Arminian readers see each worker remembered by name.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see each worker known to God. The text names Meremoth and Hakkoz without connecting them to other notices, and both traditions read the verse as shared ground about ordinary, recorded labor.

verses.text: Next to them, the Tekoites made repairs; but their nobles didn’t put their necks to the Lord’s work.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Tekoites make repairs, but their nobles do not put their necks to the Lord’s work. The narrator notes the refusal.

Arminian readers see a free refusal by some leaders, recorded honestly beside the willing work of others.
verses.reformedNotes:
The image of the neck suggests unwillingness to take up the yoke of labor. The Tekoites themselves later repair a second section (3:27).

Reformed readers see that privilege does not guarantee faithfulness. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Joiada the son of Paseah and Meshullam the son of Besodeiah repaired the old gate. They laid its beams and set up its doors, its bolts, and its bars.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joiada son of Paseah and Meshullam son of Besodeiah repair the old gate, laying its beams and setting up its doors, bolts, and bars. Another gate is restored.

Arminian readers see steady, cooperative effort.
verses.reformedNotes:
The name ‘old gate’ and its location are discussed by interpreters, and certainty is not possible from the text alone.

Reformed readers see God restoring the city through many hands. Both traditions read this as shared ground about faithful work done carefully.

verses.text: Next to them, Melatiah the Gibeonite and Jadon the Meronothite, the men of Gibeon and of Mizpah, repaired the residence of the governor beyond the River.
verses.arminianNotes:
Melatiah the Gibeonite and Jadon the Meronothite, men of Gibeon and Mizpah, repair up to the seat of the governor beyond the River. Workers come from beyond the city.

Arminian readers see willing help from nearby towns.
verses.reformedNotes:
Nehemiah 7:25 lists the children of Gibeon, where Ezra 2:20 reads Gibbar; the difference is noted, not resolved. The phrase about the governor is not fully clear.

Reformed readers see a wide gathering of God’s people. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Next to him, Uzziel the son of Harhaiah, goldsmiths, made repairs. Next to him, Hananiah, one of the perfumers, made repairs, and they fortified Jerusalem even to the wide wall.
verses.arminianNotes:
Uzziel, of the goldsmiths, and Hananiah, of the perfumers, make repairs, fortifying Jerusalem as far as the wide wall. Craftsmen leave their trades to build.

Arminian readers see people of every occupation sharing the work.
verses.reformedNotes:
Goldsmiths and perfumers were not builders by trade, which highlights the breadth of participation. The wide wall’s location is uncertain.

Reformed readers see varied gifts serving one purpose. Both traditions read this as shared ground about common labor for the community.

verses.text: Next to them, Rephaiah the son of Hur, the ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, made repairs.
verses.arminianNotes:
Rephaiah son of Hur, ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, makes repairs. A district leader works beside others.

Arminian readers see leadership expressed through personal labor, in contrast to the Tekoite nobles of verse 5.
verses.reformedNotes:
The list includes several district rulers, showing that officials took part rather than only directing.

Reformed readers see humble service among those in authority. Both traditions read this as shared ground about leaders who serve alongside the people they lead.

verses.text: Next to them, Jedaiah the son of Harumaph made repairs across from his house. Next to him, Hattush the son of Hashabneiah made repairs.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jedaiah son of Harumaph repairs across from his own house, and Hattush son of Hashabneiah works next to him. Work begins close to home.

Arminian readers see a natural and willing investment in the section that most directly concerns each family.
verses.reformedNotes:
Repairing opposite one’s own house recurs in the list (3:23, 28–30), suggesting a practical division of labor.

Reformed readers see faithfulness in one’s own place. Both traditions read this as shared ground about responsibility close at hand.

verses.text: Malchijah the son of Harim and Hasshub the son of Pahathmoab repaired another portion and the tower of the furnaces.
verses.arminianNotes:
Malchijah son of Harim and Hasshub son of Pahathmoab repair another section and the tower of the furnaces. Some take on more than one portion.

Arminian readers see diligence going beyond a single assignment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s people working steadily. The tower’s name and location are not explained, and both traditions read the verse as shared ground about generous labor on the wall.

verses.text: Next to him, Shallum the son of Hallohesh, the ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, he and his daughters made repairs.
verses.arminianNotes:
Shallum son of Hallohesh, ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, makes repairs together with his daughters. The narrator notes their part.

Arminian readers see women freely sharing in the community’s work.
verses.reformedNotes:
The mention of daughters is unusual in such lists and is recorded without comment. The text does not explain why they are named.

Reformed readers see the whole household serving. Both traditions read this as shared ground and honor the daughters’ work as the text records it.

verses.text: Hanun and the inhabitants of Zanoah repaired the valley gate. They built it, and set up its doors, its bolts, and its bars, and one thousand cubits of the wall to the dung gate.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hanun and the people of Zanoah repair the valley gate, set up its doors, bolts, and bars, and repair a thousand cubits of wall to the dung gate. A long stretch is completed.

Arminian readers see a community taking on a large share.
verses.reformedNotes:
The valley gate is where Nehemiah began his night inspection (2:13, 15). Its exact location, like many in this list, is debated.

Reformed readers see sustained labor blessed by God. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Malchijah the son of Rechab, the ruler of the district of Beth Haccherem, repaired the dung gate. He built it, and set up its doors, its bolts, and its bars.
verses.arminianNotes:
Malchijah son of Rechab, ruler of the district of Beth Haccherem, repairs the dung gate, building it and setting up its doors, bolts, and bars. Even a humble gate receives a leader’s care.

Arminian readers see willing service in an unglamorous task.
verses.reformedNotes:
The dung gate also appears in Nehemiah’s inspection (2:13). It probably served for removing refuse, though the text does not say.

Reformed readers see no task as beneath God’s servants. Both traditions read this as shared ground.
